entities.summary:
Marcus Suillius Nerullinus was a Roman senator who played a pivotal role in the governance of Rome during the reign of Emperor Claudius (41–54 CE).

As consul ordinarius in 50 CE, he worked closely with Gaius Antistius Vetus, another prominent senator, to address the growing instability in the Roman Empire. Their efforts were part of a broader effort to reform the Roman administration and strengthen the empire's military presence.

Despite his significant contributions to Roman politics, Nerullinus's life remains somewhat of a mystery, and there is ongoing debate among historians about the details of his career and the impact of his actions on Roman history.

Nerullinus's legacy can be seen in the many Roman laws and edicts that bear his name, which were designed to promote the welfare of Roman citizens and to strengthen the empire's institutions.

The legacy of Marcus Suillius Nerullinus serves as a reminder of the ongoing struggle for power and influence in the Roman Empire, and the complex web of relationships between politicians, military leaders, and the general population.

This is evident in the famous phrase "Et qui nihil fecit, nihil de se habet" ('And he who did nothing, has nothing to say of himself'), which was attributed to Nerullinus and reflects his commitment to the principles of Roman governance and his dedication to serving the Roman people.
